pages.x: Korea's Joseon kings were loyal to Ming China, which had saved them from the Japanese in the 1590s. But in the north the Manchus, led by Nurhaci, were building a new state and fighting the Ming. In 1619 Korean troops sent to help the Ming were beaten and surrendered, and in 1623 a new king, Injo, turned firmly against the Manchus.

In January 1627 Nurhaci's son Hong Taiji sent some 30,000 horsemen across the frozen Yalu. They took the border fortresses and Pyongyang, and King Injo fled to Ganghwa Island, off the coast near Seoul. With no ships to reach him and a war with the Ming to fight, the Manchus agreed to a peace that made Korea their "younger brother".

Hong Taiji grew stronger. He raided to the walls of Beijing, and the Mongols of the south submitted to him. In 1636 at Mukden he declared a new dynasty, the Qing, with himself as emperor, and demanded that Korea treat him as its lord. When Korean envoys at the ceremony refused to bow, he prepared for war.

In December 1636 Hong Taiji crossed the frozen Yalu with about 120,000 men. His horsemen rode straight past the Korean mountain fortresses that were meant to stop invaders, and reached Seoul in under two weeks. The road to Ganghwa was cut, and King Injo had to shelter in the mountain fortress of Namhansanseong.

Some 13,000 soldiers held its walls through a bitter winter, with food for fifty days. Relief armies from the provinces were beaten one by one. Inside, the court argued: some ministers wanted to die fighting for the honour of the Ming, others said the kingdom must survive. Then news came that Ganghwa had fallen, with the king's family.

On 24 February 1637 King Injo came down from the fortress in plain clothes. At Samjeondo, on the Han river, he knelt to Hong Taiji three times and bowed his head to the ground nine times. Korea broke with the Ming, paid tribute to the Qing, and sent the crown prince and his brother to Mukden as hostages.
The Qing made Korea raise a great stone at Samjeondo, carved in Manchu, Mongolian and Chinese, praising the emperor's mercy in sparing the kingdom.
pages.fx: Koreans saw it as a mark of shame. It was pulled down in 1895, when Korea broke free of the Qing, and it has been buried and set up again more than once since.

pages.x: Crown Prince Sohyeon spent eight years with the Qing, and went with them into Beijing when they took it in 1644. There he befriended the German Jesuit Adam Schall and learned of Western science and Christianity. He came home in 1645 full of new ideas, and died suddenly two months later. Many suspected poison.

Korea paid tribute to the Qing until 1895, but its scholars long believed that Korea, not Manchu-ruled China, was now the true keeper of Ming civilisation. Many women carried off as captives and later ransomed were shunned when they came home. Namhansanseong is now a World Heritage Site.
pts: Korea bowed to the Qing until 1895
Its scholars stayed loyal to the Ming in spirit
